source.title: Double Descent as a Lens for Sample Efficiency in Autoregressive vs. Discrete Diffusion Models

record.tranche_reason: The study directly tests test-loss behavior across model sizes and reports that the second descent is not pronounced in its autoregressive and discrete-diffusion language-model setup.
record.gate_note: The paper reports test BPT results for size sweeps and early stopping. Its discussion of label noise cites prior work and is not a result of this study. It does not sweep training-set size or label noise.
record.test_reason: The study measures model-size loss curves in two transformer language models and explicitly reports no second descent in its setup. These results bear directly on V1 and V4. Its comparison with best-epoch early stopping also bears on the regularization component of V6.
record.authors_conclusion: The record's paraphrase is broadly accurate. On Tiny Shakespeare, autoregressive models attain a lower optimal reported BPT with smaller capacity and fewer epochs. Diffusion models require more capacity and training, and outperform autoregressive models at embedding dimensions above 200 after 50 epochs. The authors report no second descent in their setup and suggest that pronounced image-classification double descent may not extend to generative language modeling. Diffusion BPT is an upper bound, which qualifies direct performance comparisons.
record.recipe_differences: Compares autoregressive and discrete-diffusion transformers on Tiny Shakespeare using embedding-dimension and epoch sweeps; evaluates exact autoregressive BPT against a variational bound for diffusion rather than reproducing the original studies' settings.
record.method_sensitivity: The reported onset of the first rise differs by architecture and training duration: around epoch 21 for autoregressive models and around epoch 33 for discrete diffusion models. Early stopping versus 50 epochs also changes the reported curve behavior.
record.problems: Experiments use only the small, structured Tiny Shakespeare dataset. The diffusion test metric is an upper bound on negative log-likelihood, while the autoregressive metric is exact. No uncertainty estimates are stated, and the study does not test other datasets or label-noise settings.

untested.parts: The correspondence between the test-loss peak and the size that actually interpolates the training set is not demonstrated in the supplied text.
No fixed-size fall-rise-fall trajectory over training time is reported. Epoch-dependent onset of a rise in size curves does not establish epoch-wise double descent.
Coverage beyond these two transformer language-model settings is untested; training interpolation is not independently established.
No common effective-complexity measure predicts peak locations across size, epochs, and samples.
Label-noise or variance causation, multiple peaks, and optimization over weight-decay strengths are untested. Early stopping addresses only the disappearance of the observed size-dependent rise.
No effective-parameter reparameterization of the curves is evaluated.

record.verdict_notes: Only the supplied text was assessed; plotted numerical values were unavailable. The paper calls its held-out validation loss test BPT. Early stopping selects the best held-out epoch at each size. Fixed weight decay does not test optimally tuned weight decay, and the early-stopping result does not establish the noise or variance explanation in V6.

versions.untested_parts: The study does not establish the complete fall-rise-fall curve; it reports a first rise and a threshold, but no pronounced second descent.
It varies training epochs as conditions for model-size curves but does not test test error as a function of training time at fixed model size.
The study tests only autoregressive and discrete-diffusion transformers on Tiny Shakespeare, not a broad range of model classes.
No single effective-complexity measure is evaluated as a predictor of peak location across axes.
The study does not vary label noise or tune regularization to test whether either changes or removes the peak; weight decay is applied at one stated setting.
The study does not recast complexity in terms of an effective parameter count.
